NULLITY OF MARRIAGE (ANNULMENT) — PETITION INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

DECLARATION OF PARTIES, MARRIAGE DATE, AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Nullity of Marriage (Annulment) — Petition Information Sheet concerns the marriage of Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan, who were married on June 1, 2024. It is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for nullity of marriage that would be filed in the California superior court for San Francisco County. The ground on which nullity is sought is: fraud. The factual basis asserted for that ground is: the other party concealed an existing marriage to a third person at the time of the wedding. This information sheet describes California's statutory framework for a judgment of nullity — the distinct grounds for a void marriage and for a voidable marriage, who may sue and by when, and the property, support, and custody consequences of such a judgment — as background for that filing. It is not itself a court filing, and completing it does not annul, void, or otherwise change the marital status of Jordan Alex Lee and Taylor Morgan. Only a court judgment of nullity can do that, and — for a marriage that is void rather than voidable — the marriage may already be void by operation of law whether or not any judgment is ever obtained.

VOID MARRIAGE: INCESTUOUS AND BIGAMOUS OR POLYGAMOUS MARRIAGES
California law recognizes a category of marriage that is void — automatically invalid by operation of law — as distinct from a merely voidable marriage. Two relationship-based grounds make a marriage void: incest and bigamy/polygamy. An incestuous marriage — between parents and children, ancestors and descendants of any degree, siblings of the half or whole blood, or uncles or aunts and nieces or nephews — is void from the beginning, regardless of whether the family relationship itself is legitimate or illegitimate. A bigamous or polygamous marriage — a subsequent marriage contracted by a person while a former spouse from an undissolved prior marriage is still living, with someone other than that former spouse — is illegal and void, unless one of two statutory exceptions applies: the former marriage was already dissolved or adjudged a nullity before the subsequent marriage, or the absent former spouse was not known to be living for the five years immediately preceding the subsequent marriage (or was generally reputed or believed dead when it was contracted). When one of those two bigamy exceptions applies, the subsequent marriage is not void at all — it falls instead into the voidable category addressed elsewhere in this document, with different legal consequences.

No case law was independently verified for this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

VOID FROM THE OUTSET VERSUS VOIDABLE UNTIL ANNULLED — AND THE BIGAMY EXCEPTION THAT CROSSES BETWEEN THEM
California's nullity statute treats void and voidable marriages very differently in legal effect, even though a judgment of nullity can be sought for either kind under the same part of the Family Code. A void marriage (incestuous, or bigamous/polygamous absent an exception) is invalid from its inception by operation of law; it needs no court judgment to be void, though one may still be obtained to establish that fact for the record. A voidable marriage, by contrast, is valid and has full legal effect unless and until a court adjudges it a nullity — the statute's own language is that such a marriage 'is voidable and may be adjudged a nullity,' not that it already is a nullity. The clearest illustration of this distinction sits inside the bigamy statute itself: when a person remarries reasonably believing an absent or presumed-dead former spouse is no longer living, the resulting marriage is not void bigamy at all — the statute expressly provides that this subsequent marriage 'is valid until its nullity is adjudged' under the voidable-marriage ground for an undissolved prior marriage. The same underlying fact pattern (an existing prior marriage) can therefore fall on either side of the void/voidable line depending on what the remarrying party knew or believed.

SIX STATUTORY GROUNDS FOR A VOIDABLE MARRIAGE
California Family Code § 2210 lists exactly six conditions, existing at the time of the marriage, on which a marriage is voidable and may be adjudged a nullity, in this statutory order: (a) the party seeking nullity (or on whose behalf it is sought) was under 18 at the time of marriage, unless the marriage was entered under the statutory exception for a minor who obtained a court order or parental/guardian consent permitting the marriage; (b) the other spouse from an undissolved prior marriage was living and that prior marriage was still in force, and that spouse either had been absent and not known to be living for the five years immediately preceding the later marriage, or was generally reputed or believed dead when the later marriage was contracted (this is the voidable-marriage counterpart to the bigamy ground addressed elsewhere in this document); (c) either party was of unsound mind, unless that party later freely cohabited with the other after coming to reason; (d) either party's consent was obtained by fraud, unless that party later freely cohabited with the other with full knowledge of the facts constituting the fraud; (e) either party's consent was obtained by force, unless that party later freely cohabited with the other; or (f) either party was, at the time of marriage, physically incapable of entering into the marriage state, with that incapacity continuing and appearing incurable. Grounds (c), (d), and (e) are each subject to a statutory ratification exception (freely continuing to cohabit with knowledge or after the incapacity ends) that can extinguish the ground even though it once existed.

WHO MAY SUE FOR NULLITY OF A VOIDABLE MARRIAGE, AND BY WHEN
California Family Code § 2211 separately allocates standing and a time limit for each of the six voidable-marriage grounds in § 2210, rather than applying one uniform rule. For the underage-at-marriage ground, either the party who was married under the age of legal consent may sue, within four years after reaching that age, or a parent, guardian, conservator, or other person having charge of the minor may sue at any time before the minor reaches the age of legal consent — so the minor's own window opens only after majority, while a guardian's window closes at that same point. For the undissolved-prior-marriage ground, either party to the later marriage may sue during the life of the other, or the former spouse from the earlier marriage may sue; no separate discovery-based limitations period is stated for this ground. For the unsound-mind ground, the party injured, or a relative or conservator of the party of unsound mind, may sue at any time before the death of either party. For the fraud ground, only the party whose consent was obtained by fraud may sue, within four years after discovering the facts constituting the fraud — a discovery rule, unlike the other grounds. For the force ground, only the party whose consent was obtained by force may sue, within four years after the marriage itself (not after discovery). For the physical-incapacity ground, only the injured party may sue, within four years after the marriage. This is the version of § 2211 in effect from January 1, 2026; a further 2025 amendment to the same statute becomes operative January 1, 2027 and will add a good-cause exception allowing a court to permit a late-filed petition on the force ground, while otherwise restating the same standing-and-time-limit framework.

THE PUTATIVE SPOUSE DOCTRINE AND QUASI-MARITAL PROPERTY
California law softens the consequences of a void or voidable marriage for a party who did not know the marriage was legally defective. When a marriage is determined to be void or voidable and the court finds that either party, or both, believed in good faith that the marriage was valid, the court must declare that party or those parties a 'putative spouse.' If property division is in issue, the court then divides — under the same property-division rules that apply to a community-property estate — the property acquired during the union that would have been community or quasi-community property had the marriage not been void or voidable, but only upon the request of a party who has been declared a putative spouse. This property is called 'quasi-marital property.' A party who lacked a good-faith belief the marriage was valid is not entitled to this treatment. The court may also expressly reserve jurisdiction and divide this quasi-marital property at a later time rather than in the nullity judgment itself.

SUPPORT AND CUSTODY CONSEQUENCES OF A NULLITY JUDGMENT — WHERE NULLITY DIFFERS FROM, AND MATCHES, DISSOLUTION
A nullity judgment's practical consequences do not track dissolution's default rules uniformly — some are conditioned on putative-spouse status and some are not. Spousal support is conditioned: the court may order support during the pendency of a nullity proceeding or upon the nullity judgment, in the same manner as if the marriage had not been void or voidable, but only if the party who would benefit from the order is found to be a putative spouse. A party without a good-faith belief the marriage was valid is not eligible for support under this provision, which is a real point of divergence from an ordinary dissolution, where spousal support is not conditioned on a party's good-faith belief in the marriage's validity in the first place. Property division is likewise conditioned on putative-spouse status, as described in a separate clause of this document, and property divided as quasi-marital property remains liable for the parties' debts to the same extent as if it had been community or quasi-community property. Child custody, by contrast, is not conditioned on putative-spouse status or treated any differently at all: in a nullity proceeding, custody of the children is determined according to the same Family Code division that governs custody in a dissolution proceeding, so a marriage's nullity does not itself change how a court approaches custody.

THE LEGAL EFFECT OF ANY NULLITY JUDGMENT, AND A FAULT-BASED LIMIT ON ATTORNEY'S FEES UNIQUE TO NULLITY
Whether a marriage is void or voidable, a judgment of nullity has the same basic legal effect: it restores the parties to the status of unmarried persons, and it is conclusive only as to the parties to the proceeding and those claiming under them — not conclusive against the whole world. California law also allows a court to grant attorney's fees and costs in a nullity proceeding, but attaches a fault-based limitation that has no counterpart in an ordinary dissolution proceeding: in a proceeding based on a voidable marriage, a party may recover fees and costs only if that party is found innocent of fraud or wrongdoing in inducing or entering into the marriage, and free from knowledge, at the time, of a prior marriage or other impediment to the marriage for which nullity is sought. A party who was at fault in bringing about the very defect that makes the marriage voidable — for example, the party who committed the fraud, rather than the party who was defrauded — is therefore not eligible for a fee award under this provision, even though either party could otherwise be a party to the proceeding.

expectedJSON.body: California Family Code § 2211 separately allocates standing and a time limit for each of the six voidable-marriage grounds in § 2210, rather than applying one uniform rule. For the underage-at-marriage ground, either the party who was married under the age of legal consent may sue, within four years after reaching that age, or a parent, guardian, conservator, or other person having charge of the minor may sue at any time before the minor reaches the age of legal consent — so the minor's own window opens only after majority, while a guardian's window closes at that same point. For the undissolved-prior-marriage ground, either party to the later marriage may sue during the life of the other, or the former spouse from the earlier marriage may sue; no separate discovery-based limitations period is stated for this ground. For the unsound-mind ground, the party injured, or a relative or conservator of the party of unsound mind, may sue at any time before the death of either party. For the fraud ground, only the party whose consent was obtained by fraud may sue, within four years after discovering the facts constituting the fraud — a discovery rule, unlike the other grounds. For the force ground, only the party whose consent was obtained by force may sue, within four years after the marriage itself (not after discovery). For the physical-incapacity ground, only the injured party may sue, within four years after the marriage. This is the version of § 2211 in effect from January 1, 2026; a further 2025 amendment to the same statute becomes operative January 1, 2027 and will add a good-cause exception allowing a court to permit a late-filed petition on the force ground, while otherwise restating the same standing-and-time-limit framework.

expectedJSON.body: California law softens the consequences of a void or voidable marriage for a party who did not know the marriage was legally defective. When a marriage is determined to be void or voidable and the court finds that either party, or both, believed in good faith that the marriage was valid, the court must declare that party or those parties a 'putative spouse.' If property division is in issue, the court then divides — under the same property-division rules that apply to a community-property estate — the property acquired during the union that would have been community or quasi-community property had the marriage not been void or voidable, but only upon the request of a party who has been declared a putative spouse. This property is called 'quasi-marital property.' A party who lacked a good-faith belief the marriage was valid is not entitled to this treatment. The court may also expressly reserve jurisdiction and divide this quasi-marital property at a later time rather than in the nullity judgment itself.

expectedJSON.body: A nullity judgment's practical consequences do not track dissolution's default rules uniformly — some are conditioned on putative-spouse status and some are not. Spousal support is conditioned: the court may order support during the pendency of a nullity proceeding or upon the nullity judgment, in the same manner as if the marriage had not been void or voidable, but only if the party who would benefit from the order is found to be a putative spouse. A party without a good-faith belief the marriage was valid is not eligible for support under this provision, which is a real point of divergence from an ordinary dissolution, where spousal support is not conditioned on a party's good-faith belief in the marriage's validity in the first place. Property division is likewise conditioned on putative-spouse status, as described in a separate clause of this document, and property divided as quasi-marital property remains liable for the parties' debts to the same extent as if it had been community or quasi-community property. Child custody, by contrast, is not conditioned on putative-spouse status or treated any differently at all: in a nullity proceeding, custody of the children is determined according to the same Family Code division that governs custody in a dissolution proceeding, so a marriage's nullity does not itself change how a court approaches custody.

expectedJSON.body: Whether a marriage is void or voidable, a judgment of nullity has the same basic legal effect: it restores the parties to the status of unmarried persons, and it is conclusive only as to the parties to the proceeding and those claiming under them — not conclusive against the whole world. California law also allows a court to grant attorney's fees and costs in a nullity proceeding, but attaches a fault-based limitation that has no counterpart in an ordinary dissolution proceeding: in a proceeding based on a voidable marriage, a party may recover fees and costs only if that party is found innocent of fraud or wrongdoing in inducing or entering into the marriage, and free from knowledge, at the time, of a prior marriage or other impediment to the marriage for which nullity is sought. A party who was at fault in bringing about the very defect that makes the marriage voidable — for example, the party who committed the fraud, rather than the party who was defrauded — is therefore not eligible for a fee award under this provision, even though either party could otherwise be a party to the proceeding.

citations.quote: The effect of a judgment of nullity of marriage is to restore the parties to the status of unmarried persons. (b) A judgment of nullity of marriage is conclusive only as to the parties to the proceeding and those claiming under them.
